content: Tuberculosis (TB) infection testing is not mandatory for initiating TB preventive treatment (TPT) in adolescents living with HIV. However, if available, it can be used to assess eligibility for TPT in this population. Infants under 12 months of age who are living with HIV and do not exhibit TB symptoms should only receive TPT if they have a history of contact with a person with TB, and active TB disease has been excluded. Infants, children, and adolescents living with HIV who report symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or other signs suggestive of TB should be evaluated for TB disease and other conditions. If TB disease is ruled out following clinical evaluation or national guidelines, TPT should be offered. Clinical algorithms are used to guide treatment decisions in children suspected of having TB. For asymptomatic infants under 1 year of age living with HIV, TPT is only recommended if they are household contacts of a person with TB. Tuberculin skin tests (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) may help identify individuals living with HIV who would benefit most from TPT. Chest X-rays (CXR) may also be used in people living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy (ART) before starting TPT. Symptoms such as cough, fever, night sweats, hemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain, shortness of breath, or fatigue may indicate TB disease. In children under 5 years, additional symptoms like anorexia, failure to thrive, poor appetite, or reduced activity should also be considered. TB disease must be ruled out in individuals with clinical manifestations suggestive of TB before starting TPT. Pregnancy and a history of TB are not contraindications for TPT. However, conditions such as acute or chronic hepatitis, peripheral neuropathy (if isoniazid is used), or heavy alcohol consumption should be carefully considered. The choice of TPT regimen depends on factors such as age, drug susceptibility, risk of toxicity, availability, and patient preferences. TPT regimens recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for children and adolescents include: 6 or 9 months of daily isoniazid (6H or 9H) for all ages. 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP) for those aged 2 years and older. 3 months of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin (3HR) for all ages. 1 month of daily isoniazid plus rifapentine (1HP) for those aged 13 years and older. 4 months of daily rifampicin (4R) for all ages. The 3HR regimen is preferred for children due to its shorter duration, better tolerability, and availability of child-friendly dispersible fixed-dose combination (FDC) formulations. For children living with HIV on ART regimens such as lopinavir/ritonavir, dolutegravir, or nevirapine, the 6H regimen remains the most suitable option until further data on rifapentine-based regimens become available. Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplementation is recommended for individuals at risk of peripheral neuropathy, such as those with malnutrition, HIV, renal failure, diabetes, or those who are pregnant or breastfeeding. Exclusively breastfed infants on isoniazid should also receive vitamin B6 supplementation. For household contacts of individuals with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) or isoniazid monoresistance, the risk of TB infection is higher. WHO suggests using levofloxacin for 6 months as TPT in these cases, along with other TB medicines like ethambutol or ethionamide if tolerated. Clinical follow-up for 2 years is recommended, with active investigation of any emerging TB symptoms and initiation of treatment as needed.
